Executive Summary: Plastics are increasingly used across industries, driving continual growth in production leading to more landfill and incineration waste. The multi-university center for the Chemical Upcycling of Waste Plastics (CUWP) was established to research and develop technologies that divert plastic waste from end-of-life disposal and convert it to valuable products. CUWP’s research focused on advancing plastic pyrolysis, catalytic upgrading of pyrolysis oils, and solvent based recycling of multilayer films. Pyrolysis breaks down polyolefin plastics to produce a mixture of hydrocarbons that can be converted into chemicals such as aromatics and surfactants. CUWP demonstrated this process at the pilot scale, and economic analyses show that chemically recycling plastics into surfactants can reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 60% compared to conventional surfactant production, with an estimated to payback period of under 5 years. CUWP also developed a technology called STRAP, a solvent-based method that separates multilayer plastic films, commonly seen in food packaging, into reusable plastic streams with properties comparable to virgin materials. Alongside technological development, CUWP emphasized public education and outreach. The public choosing to recycle plastics rather than throw them away is the first step of chemical recycling. K-12 lesson plans, university courses, and undergraduate research programs were created to improve public understanding of plastic recycling and encourage participation in local recycling programs. These efforts support the broader goal of strengthening U.S. recycling infrastructure and expanding the range of plastics that can be sustainably reused. Table of Contents: 1.
